cues.text: Your computer works with bits.
A bit is the smallest piece of information, and it is always either 0 or 1.
Every photo, message and game on your computer is a long list of 0s and 1s.
A quantum computer uses qubits, short for quantum bits.
A qubit is a tiny physical thing, such as a very small electric part or a single atom.
A qubit can be in superposition: a mix of 0 and 1 at the same time, until we measure it.
Picture a coin spinning on a table.
While it spins, it is not heads or tails.
When it stops, it becomes one of them.
Measuring a qubit is like stopping the coin: the superposition ends, and you get a normal 0 or 1.
Qubits can also be linked: this is called entanglement.
The result of one qubit is connected to the result of the other, even when they are far apart.
Now picture two linked coins.
Nobody knows how they will land.
In one simple case, every time one lands on heads, the other lands on heads too.
Other links are possible, for example one heads and the other tails.
Entanglement lets many qubits work as one big system instead of many separate parts.
So why can this be faster?
Many people think a quantum computer tries every answer at once.
That is not true, because at the end you only get one answer.
The real trick is interference.
The program is made so wrong answers cancel each other out.
The right answer grows stronger.
Think of waves in water.
When two waves meet, they can make one bigger wave, or they can cancel each other out.
This trick only works for problems with a special math pattern.
That is why a quantum computer is not a faster laptop.
For email, videos and games, a normal computer is better.
Quantum computers are useful for a small group of problems.
They can copy how atoms and molecules behave, and solve some special math problems.
One example is the problem behind much of today's encryption.
The biggest enemy of a qubit is noise: any tiny disturbance from the outside world.
A little heat, a small shake or a weak radio signal can push a qubit out of its superposition.
Then the information is lost, and the calculation has an error.
A qubit in Google's Willow chip keeps its information for only about 100 microseconds.
That is a tiny part of one second.
On its own, a qubit loses what it holds long before a big calculation could finish.
To reduce noise, many quantum computers are kept extremely cold.
IBM cools its chips to about minus 273 degrees Celsius.
That is colder than outer space, which is about minus 270 degrees Celsius.
At this temperature, atoms almost stop, so there is very little heat to disturb the qubits.
Even with all this care, qubits make mistakes far more often than normal computers.
A normal computer can fix errors by keeping copies.
A quantum computer cannot do this: the laws of physics do not allow an unknown qubit to be copied.
It also cannot simply look at a qubit, because looking ends the superposition.
The solution is error correction: the information of one reliable qubit is spread across many physical qubits.
The physical qubits are the real, noisy ones in the machine.
Together they make one logical qubit, the reliable one that the program uses.
Some extra qubits keep checking whether their neighbors still agree, without reading the information itself.
When a check shows a problem, a normal computer works out which qubit went wrong and corrects it.
This way, the logical qubit can keep its information longer than any one of its physical qubits.
Error correction only helps if the physical qubits are already good enough.
If they are too noisy, adding more qubits adds more errors than it fixes.
This border is called the threshold.
For many years, no machine was clearly on the right side of it.
In December 2024, Google showed clearly that error correction gets better as the machine grows.
On its Willow chip, the team stored one logical qubit on a 3×3 square of qubits that hold the data.
Extra qubits between them did the checks.
Then they used a 5×5 square, then a 7×7 square.
Each time the square grew, the error rate was cut in half.
This was the threshold result that scientists had waited for: bigger machines can become more reliable, not less.
Earlier speed records had a weakness.
They were jobs with no practical use, and nobody could easily check the answers.
In October 2025, Google ran a program called Quantum Echoes.
Google says it was 13,000 times faster than on one of the world's fastest computers.
Its result can be checked.
The team ran a series of steps on the qubits.
They disturbed one qubit, then ran all the steps again in the opposite order.
They measured the signal that came back.
It is called an echo, like a shout that comes back in a mountain valley.
Google calls this verifiable quantum advantage.
A quantum computer does a job much faster than normal computers, and the result can be checked.
Normal computers are too slow to check the full calculation.
Instead, another quantum computer of the same quality can run it again and should get the same answer.
When you read quantum news, ask one question: is it proven, claimed or only planned?
Publishing in a journal is only one check.
Proven: Google measured the error rates on its chip directly, and the journal Nature published the data.
Claimed: Quantum Echoes was also published in Nature.
But the 13,000 number is Google's estimate of the time a normal computer would need, not a measurement.
Also, no other quantum computer has repeated the result yet.
Planned: In November 2026, IBM announced plans for Nighthawk r3, a chip for 2027.
It will have 2,034 physical qubits, but programs can use only 520.
The others are helper parts that connect and support those 520.
These are plans, not finished machines, and even the 520 qubits are physical, not logical.
Today, quantum computers are tools for science experiments, not for everyday business.
The most promising use is studying molecules and materials.
Atoms and electrons follow quantum rules.
A normal computer needs huge amounts of memory to copy how they behave.
A quantum computer follows the same rules naturally.
RIKEN, a research center in Japan, worked with IBM.
They connected an IBM quantum computer to Fugaku, a very large computer in Japan.
They used them to study a molecule with iron atoms in it.
The quantum computer did the part it is good at, and Fugaku did the rest of the calculation.
This is the realistic picture for the next years: quantum computers and big normal computers working as a team.
Two famous promises are still far away: curing diseases and breaking internet encryption.
Scientists already design new medicines with other methods, such as lab tests and normal computers.
One day, quantum computers might help by copying large molecules from the body in great detail.
That would need many logical qubits working without mistakes for a long time.
No machine is close to that today.
Much of the internet is protected by RSA.
RSA is safe because one math problem is very hard for normal computers.
Everyone can see a very big public number.
It was made by multiplying two secret prime numbers.
The hard problem is to find those two prime numbers when you only know the big number.
A large quantum computer could solve it.
A Google researcher worked out that breaking common RSA would need fewer than one million noisy physical qubits.
They would need to run for less than a week.
Today's best machines have roughly 100 to 1,000 qubits.
In our lesson on computer safety, encryption was the lock that protects information.
So why are countries changing their locks now, years before such a machine exists?
Attackers can save locked information today and open it when a quantum computer is ready.
This is called harvest now, decrypt later.
Health records, government secrets and bank information must stay secret for many years, so they need new protection now.
The new locks are called post-quantum encryption.
They use new math problems that are believed to be hard even for quantum computers.
They run on normal computers and phones, so nobody needs a quantum computer to use them.
The US standards office NIST has already published the first standards.
This year, NIST set its final dates.
After 2030, old methods such as RSA become out of date.
After 2035, they are no longer allowed under NIST's rules.
AI is already helping quantum computers today, in real, published work.
It helps with three jobs: finding errors, tuning the machine and designing programs.
The first job is finding errors.
The extra qubits that do the checks send a stream of messy results.
A normal computer must quickly work out which qubit went wrong.
This is called decoding.
In 2024, Google DeepMind and Google Quantum AI published AlphaQubit.
It is an AI decoder.
It found errors more accurately than the best earlier methods.
The first AlphaQubit was too slow for a real machine.
The machine repeats its checks about a million times every second.
Later, the team shared a faster one, which the authors say works in real time.
The second job is tuning.
A quantum computer has many control settings, like the knobs on an old radio.
These settings slowly move away from their best values.
Today, automatic programs and experts set them.
To fix the slow change, the error checks must stop for a new setup.
Google researchers built an AI agent that uses reinforcement learning.
This means it gets better by trying things and getting a reward.
It keeps changing more than a thousand settings while the machine keeps working.
So the error checks do not need to stop.
It uses the error checks as its score.
In their tests, it reduced the logical error rate by about 20 percent more.
This was on a machine already set by programs and experts.
The third job is design.
AI can design better quantum circuits, the step-by-step programs that a quantum computer runs.
In an error-corrected machine, one kind of step, the T gate, costs much more than the others.
The machine cannot do this step reliably in the normal way.
So each T gate needs many extra qubits and extra steps.
Google DeepMind and Quantinuum presented AlphaTensor-Quantum.
This AI rewrites the circuits so that they need fewer T gates.
On some tests, it cut their number by half or more.
Fewer expensive steps mean that a machine can do useful work sooner.
Will quantum computers make AI better?
The answer today is: mostly unknown.
In 2025, the bank HSBC and IBM reported better test scores for a machine-learning model.
The model learned from trading data that was changed on a real IBM quantum computer.
It was one small study, not proof that quantum computers make AI better in general.
One big problem is data.
AI learns from huge amounts of data, and putting that data into qubits is slow.
This can use up the time that a quantum computer saves.
So today, the help goes mostly one way.
AI helps quantum computers much more than quantum computers help AI.
